steps.text: Part 2 of 3: Discovered attacks and discovered check. This part covers Set it up or stop it; Mixed test; A real game. Each part is short on purpose: finish one, play a game or take a break, and come back.

steps.caption: A real game: Negi - Richter, Bundesliga 2013-14. White to move recaptures on f4. Watch where the bishop lands.

line.say: The bishop takes the pawn and lands on the f-file, directly in front of its own rook.
Black strikes at the bishop on c4. The bishop on f4 stays where it is.

claims.statement: After the recapture, the rook on f1 stands directly behind the bishop on f4.
The bishop stands on f4 after the recapture.

steps.chapter: Set it up or stop it

steps.text: **Building a discovery.** Put a slider on a line, put your own piece in front of it, and aim the line at something that matters: a king, a queen, a loose piece. Now the front piece can move whenever it has a good move, and the opponent must keep watching that line. [H] Such a battery may be worth more as a standing threat than as a quick strike; I have not measured this.

steps.caption: Prevention first. Black to move in a game with the queens on the same rank and a white bishop between them. Castling looks natural.

line.say: Black castles. The king now stands on g8, on the diagonal of the bishop.
The bishop takes h7 with check and uncovers the white queen's attack on the black queen.
The king takes the bishop.
The queen takes the queen.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine rates castling at least 400 centipawns below the best move.
Before the bishop moves, the bishop on d3 blocks the white queen's line to c3.
After castling and Bxh7+, the white queen attacks the black queen on c3.

steps.caption: The same position with a better plan: first move the target off the line, then castle.

line.say: The queen steps off the rank. The bishop's trick no longer has a target.
White plays on, but there is no discovery to fear.
Now castling does not walk into a discovered attack.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine's best move is one of these three.

steps.caption: Black to move. Taking the pawn on b2 with the queen is tempting. Look at what stands on the second rank.

line.say: The queen grabs a pawn and steps onto the second rank, where only the white bishop stands between the queens.
The bishop moves with check and uncovers the white queen's attack.
The king takes the bishop.
The white queen takes the black queen.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine rates ...Qxb2 at least 400 centipawns below the best move.
Before the bishop moves, the bishop on c2 blocks the white queen's line to b2.
After ...Qxb2 and Bh7+, the white queen attacks the black queen on b2.

steps.caption: Black to move. The white knight on e7 gives check, and two black pieces can capture it.

line.say: The knight takes the knight, and the queen stays on the c-file, in the line of the white queen.
The bishop takes f7 with check and uncovers the white queen's attack on the black queen.
The rook takes the bishop.
The white queen takes the black queen.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine rates Nxe7 at least 600 centipawns below the best move.
Before the bishop moves, the bishop on c4 blocks the white queen's line to c5.
After Nxe7 and Bxf7+, the white queen attacks the black queen on c5.

steps.caption: The same position, with the right capture: the queen takes the knight.

line.say: The queen takes the knight and leaves c5, so a bishop move has no queen behind it to aim at.
The white bishop takes a pawn instead.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine's best move is Qxe7.

steps.caption: White to move. Rook to e1 looks natural. Look at the b6 bishop, the black queen and the white queen on c6.

line.say: The rook joins the e-file, behind its own bishop. It does nothing about the black bishop's trick.
The bishop takes that bishop and uncovers the black queen's attack on the white queen.
White takes back, but the queen is still attacked.
The queen takes the queen.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine rates Rfe1 at least 250 centipawns below the best move.
At depth 16 the engine's best move is one of these two.

steps.text: **Stopping one.** Before you move, scan the lines through your king and queen. Is an enemy slider aiming along one, with his own piece in front? Ask what that piece could do next, and pick a move that survives: move the target, block the line, or remove the back piece. Castling on autopilot and grabbing a pawn are the usual ways in. Several of the next boards come from Lichess puzzle data (CC0); the earliest in this lesson are constructed.

No labels from here. About one Lichess puzzle in twenty carries the discovered-attack theme (311,174 of 6,157,341, our count from the CC0 file) [V]. Puzzles are chosen because they hold a tactic, so this is not how often you will meet one in your own games [I]. Expect positions where nothing is hidden, and where the right answer is that there is no tactic.

A game between two strong players: Negi (White, rated 2671) against Richter (Black, 2473), Bundesliga 2013-14, round 14, 5 April 2014, drawn [V, TWIC record in our data]. White has set a battery on the f-file. Watch how a sacrifice drags the black king in front of it.

steps.caption: White to move (move 13). Queen and knight aim at f7. Count what each side gives up.

line.say: The queen joins the knight in attacking f7.
Black attacks the knight.
The knight takes f7 anyway, a pawn.
The rook takes the knight.
The queen takes the rook, with check.
The king takes the queen. White has traded a queen and a knight for a rook and a pawn.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine rates the starting position within one pawn of equal.
After Qh5, two white pieces attack f7.

steps.caption: The game continued. The black king stands on f7, on the f-file, with the bishop and the rook in line behind it.

line.say: The bishop moves away and the rook gives check, and from c7 the bishop attacks the queen on d8.
Black blocks the file with the knight.
The bishop takes the queen. White has the queen back.
The bishop takes the bishop.
White checks again. The game ended in a draw.
The king steps aside.

claims.statement: At depth 16 the engine's best move is Bc7+.
Bc7+ followed by Bxd8 wins material along the engine's line.
Before the bishop moves, the bishop blocks the rook's line to f7.
After the bishop leaves f4, the rook attacks the king on f7.

steps.text: The discovery did not win the game. The engine (depth 16) rated the position slightly worse for White before it and close to level after [V]. A discovery can regain material or save a game as well as win one.

**Check yourself.** Can you name the three pieces, and say what job the front piece needs? Can you say when it fails: the line is shut, the front piece has no job, or the opponent takes the back piece first? Remember to scan every line from a back piece.

steps.prompt: Explain discovered attacks to a friend who has only just learned the moves. Use your own words and include one position you could set up on a board.

fields.label: The idea in your own words
A position you could set up on a board

steps.text: **One model answer.** Set up the position of the third demonstration: front piece the bishop on e4, back piece the rook on e1, target the queen on e8. The bishop captures on h7 with check, so Black must answer the check before saving the queen. It fails if the king stands on h8 (no check) or the rook stands on d1 (no line). The usual mistake is to look only at the piece that moves.

steps.prompt: How close was your own position to this model answer? Say what you would change.

steps.text: **Remember.** To build a discovery, put a slider on a line with your own piece in front, aimed at something that matters. To stop one, scan the lines through your king and queen before you move, then move the target, block the line, or remove the back piece. It fails if the line is shut, the front piece has no job, or the back piece is taken first.
